title: Landmark Trial Shows 4 in 5 Rectal Cancer Patients Can Avoid Major Surgery
excerpt: The STAR-TREC trial, published in The Lancet Oncology, found that chemoradiotherapy allowed most early-stage rectal cancer patients to keep their rectum and skip radical surgery.
body:
• The STAR-TREC trial found that chemoradiotherapy allowed 4 in 5 early-stage rectal cancer patients to keep their rectum and avoid radical surgery.
  • The international trial recruited over 500 patients across five countries and compared organ-preserving treatments against the current standard of total rectal removal.
  • Five weeks of chemoradiotherapy proved more effective than five days of radiotherapy alone, with patients experiencing minimal side effects.
  • Results were published in The Lancet Oncology; researchers will follow patients for three more years to monitor recurrence and survival.

A landmark clinical trial has found that most patients with early-stage rectal cancer can be successfully treated without the radical surgery that has been the standard of care for decades — a finding researchers say could transform treatment for thousands of patients worldwide each year.

The STAR-TREC trial, coordinated by the University of Birmingham and co-led by University College London and the University of Leeds, recruited over 500 patients across five countries including the UK, the Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark, and Belgium. The results, published in The Lancet Oncology, show that chemoradiotherapy — combining chemotherapy with radiotherapy — allowed four in five patients to keep their rectum entirely.

A Treatment That Preserves Quality of Life

Currently, patients diagnosed with early-stage rectal cancer typically undergo major surgery to remove their entire rectum. The procedure can lead to life-altering side effects including permanent colostomy bags, bowel dysfunction, and sexual and urinary problems.

The trial tested two organ-preserving approaches against this surgical standard: five weeks of chemoradiotherapy and five days of shorter-course radiotherapy. Patients who received either alternative underwent radical surgery only if their tumour was not responding sufficiently. Where small areas of cancer persisted, surgeons performed rectum-preserving operations — smaller, less invasive procedures with fewer complications.

"For decades we've asked patients to accept the loss of their rectum — and often a permanent stoma — as the price of curing their cancer. These results suggest that for many people, this price no longer has to be paid."

— Prof. Simon Bach, Co-Chief Investigator, STAR-TREC Trial, UCL

After 12 months, five weeks of chemoradiotherapy emerged as the more effective approach. Patients in this group were less likely to require radical surgery than those who received five days of radiotherapy, and they experienced minimal severe short-term side effects.

Why This Matters

About 4,100 people in the UK alone are diagnosed with early-stage rectal cancer each year, a number that is growing as bowel screening programmes detect more cancers at earlier stages. In India, colorectal cancer incidence has been rising, particularly in urban populations, with the Indian Council of Medical Research projecting continued increases through the decade.

"These exciting results are an example of how a smarter, kinder radiotherapy treatment may allow patients to avoid the need for major surgery," said David Sebag-Montefiore, co-chief investigator and professor of clinical oncology at the University of Leeds. "It is gratifying that patients experienced a relatively low level of severe short-term side effects."

Michelle Mitchell, Cancer Research UK's chief executive, called the findings potentially "life-changing for thousands of people," noting that better screening has improved detection but not made treatment any easier for patients.

What Comes Next

The research team will follow patients for the next three years to monitor whether cancer is more likely to return without radical surgery and whether there is a difference in long-term survival. If the results hold, researchers hope organ-preserving chemoradiotherapy will become a standard treatment option available to all eligible patients.

Brian, one of the trial participants, said his consultant had told him radical surgery would likely mean a permanent colostomy bag. After opting for the trial and undergoing five days of intensive radiotherapy, subsequent CT scans, MRI scans, and endoscopies have all shown no trace of cancer. "I'm a massive fan of clinical trials," he said. "Success stories like mine wouldn't be possible without research into better and kinder treatments."

The trial was funded by Cancer Research UK and Stand Up To Cancer, and the full study — led by Simon P. Bach and colleagues — is available in The Lancet Oncology.
